claim: The short phoneme /ə/ has a recurrent [u]-like realization when adjacent to labials, /r/ or emphatic /ṛ/, /w/, or /q/.
normalized_environment: SCHWA realized [u]-like adjacent to LABIAL/RHOTIC/W/Q contexts
scope: major schwa allophony; tendencies rather than categorical phonetic rules
exceptions_or_counterexamples: The author says the realization 'usually' occurs in these environments and explicitly notes interspeaker/nonlocal conditioning of schwa quality elsewhere; do not encode as exceptionless.

claim: Short [u] is not only an allophone of /ə/: historical short /u/ survives in a small lexical set, and short /u/ also occurs in loans. The grammar therefore distinguishes environmentally conditioned [u]-quality schwa from lexically or historically retained short [u].
normalized_environment: SHORT_U marginal: HISTORICAL_RETENTION + LOAN stratum; not reducible to SCHWA_ALLOPHONE
scope: small inherited lexical set plus loans
exceptions_or_counterexamples: Both kull and kəll are attested according to the grammar's transcription discussion, so even a retained item can vary.
section: 4.3.2 /ə/ with the quality of [u]; transcription conventions

time_scope: modern Jewish Gabes with Classical Arabic comparison
claim: Etymological diphthongs are regularly contracted in Jewish Gabes: Classical Arabic /ay/ generally corresponds to /ī/, and /aw/ to /ū/.
exceptions_or_counterexamples: The grammar calls these shifts very regular rather than exceptionless; a separate secondary process can re-diphthongize resulting /ī/ in particular guttural/emphatic environments.
table_figure: Table 7: Diphthongs in CA, Jewish Wad-Souf, and Jewish Gabes

claim: Long /ī/ created by historical /ay/ contraction may undergo secondary diphthongization with /ə/ when it occurs between two guttural or emphatic consonants.
normalized_environment: LONG_I secondary diphthongization between GUTTURAL/EMPHATIC consonants
exceptions_or_counterexamples: The author says the long vowel 'tends' to be diphthongized, so this is a conditioned tendency rather than an absolute output rule.

claim: Short /o/ has an unusually restricted and partly unstable distribution. The grammar finds only one minimal pair establishing a possible phonemic contrast and notes alternation with /u/, /a/, or /ə/ in cognate/parallel forms, so its phonemic status is explicitly uncertain.

source_forms.variation: ḍāṛ–ḍoṛt / ḍuṛt 'to roam'; ṣām–ṣomt / ṣamt 'to fast'
source_forms.phonemic_evidence: only one minimal pair reported in grammar

formal_environment: short o in limited lexical/morphological environments
normalized_environment: SHORT_O = MARGINAL/UNCERTAIN phoneme; distribution limited and alternates with other short qualities
exceptions_or_counterexamples: The existence of a minimal pair prevents simply classifying every [o] as allophonic, while its extreme rarity prevents treating /o/ as distributionally equivalent to /a,ə/.
